words.def: Careful to spend little money and avoid waste; (of a meal) simple and cheap.
ex: My grandparents lived [frugal] lives, but they were never unhappy.
By being [frugal] for two years, they saved enough for a deposit.
We had a [frugal] supper of bread, cheese and soup.
words.nuance: Frugal and thrifty are positive: sensible, avoiding waste. Stingy, tight-fisted and miserly are negative: unwilling to spend or give even when you should. Parsimonious is formal and usually critical — extreme reluctance to spend.
words.ety: Latin frugalis 'economical', from frux 'fruit, value'.

prec.s: My grandmother was ___ rather than mean: she reused every jar but never let a guest leave hungry.
prec.why: Frugal is a virtue — careful spending without meanness — which the second half of the sentence shows. Stingy, miserly and tight-fisted all criticise reluctance to give.

words.def: Extremely unwilling to spend money or use resources; (in science) using as few assumptions as possible.
ex: The [parsimonious] landlord refused to fix the heating.
Critics attacked the government's [parsimonious] funding of the arts.
Scientists prefer the most [parsimonious] explanation that fits the data.
words.nuance: Parsimonious is a formal, critical word for meanness with money. Its scientific sense (the simplest explanation, as in Occam's razor) is neutral and positive.
words.ety: Latin parsimonia, from parcere 'to spare'.

prec.s: Faced with two theories that fit the data, scientists usually prefer the more ___ one.
prec.why: In science, 'parsimonious' (principle of parsimony) means requiring the fewest assumptions. Frugal and economical are about money; austere means severe and plain.

words.def: Generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival or someone less powerful.
ex: She was [magnanimous] in victory, praising her opponent's campaign.
It was [magnanimous] of him to forgive the people who had betrayed him.
The team showed great [magnanimity] after the controversial result.
words.nuance: Magnanimous is about generosity of spirit, especially from a position of strength (after winning, when wronged). Generous is broader and often about money; benevolent is about kindly wishing others well.
words.ety: Latin magnus 'great' + animus 'soul'.

prec.s: After winning the election by a landslide, she was ___ towards her defeated rival.
prec.why: Magnanimous is the word for generosity of spirit towards a defeated rival or offender. Benevolent means kindly in general; lavish means extravagant; charitable relates to giving to the needy or judging kindly.

words.def: Kind and well-meaning; wanting to help others.
ex: The old man smiled at the children in a [benevolent] way.
Some argue that a [benevolent] dictatorship is still a dictatorship.
The hospital was funded by a [benevolent] society in the 1890s.
words.nuance: Benevolent describes goodwill, often from someone in a position of power (a benevolent ruler). Benign is gentle and harmless (also medical: not cancerous). Opposite: malevolent.
words.ety: Latin bene 'well' + volens 'wishing'.

prec.s: The factory owner saw himself as a ___ father figure, providing housing and schools for his workers.
prec.why: Benevolent describes a well-meaning person, especially one with power. Benign means harmless; beneficial describes things that have good effects; benefactor is a noun (a person who gives money).

words.def: Having or showing a wish to do evil or harm to others.
ex: The villain stared at her with [malevolent] eyes.
Some hackers are merely curious; others are truly [malevolent].
There was a [malevolent] silence in the room after the accusation.
words.nuance: Malevolent means actively wishing harm — an inner disposition, often with a sinister feel. Malicious describes actions or intent meant to hurt (malicious gossip, malicious software).
words.ety: Latin male 'badly' + volens 'wishing'.

prec.s: In the horror film, the house seems to be inhabited by some ___ presence.
prec.why: Malevolent describes a sinister, evil-wishing force or being. Malicious is for intentional harmful acts (malicious damage); malignant is medical or about spreading evil; malcontent is a noun for a dissatisfied person.

words.def: Fond of company; sociable. (Of animals) living in groups.
ex: My brother is [gregarious] and loves big parties; I prefer small dinners.
She's a warm, [gregarious] woman who knows everyone in the village.
Sheep are [gregarious] animals and get stressed when alone.
words.nuance: Gregarious means actively enjoying the company of others. Convivial describes a cheerful atmosphere or event; affable means pleasant and easy to talk to, even one-to-one.
words.ety: Latin gregarius, from grex 'flock'.

prec.s: Being naturally ___, he found working from home alone for months almost unbearable.
prec.why: Gregarious means needing and enjoying company — so isolation is painful. Convivial describes atmospheres; garrulous means over-talkative; affable means friendly and easy to talk to.

words.def: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily; reluctant to speak.
ex: He is [reticent] about his time in the army.
The normally [reticent] actress spoke openly about her illness.
Her [reticence] was often mistaken for arrogance.
words.nuance: Reticent means holding back information or feelings, usually about a specific topic ('reticent about her past'). Taciturn describes a person who habitually says very little. Careful: many people misuse reticent to mean 'reluctant' in general.
words.ety: Latin reticere 'to keep silent', from tacere 'to be silent'.

prec.s: She talks freely about her career but is ___ about her private life.
prec.why: 'Reticent about' a topic is the precise use: unwilling to share on that subject. Taciturn is a general trait (saying little about anything); laconic means using few words; mute means unable or refusing to speak at all.

words.def: Habitually saying very little; uncommunicative.
ex: Her [taciturn] father rarely spoke at dinner.
The [taciturn] farmer answered every question with a nod or a shrug.
Despite his [taciturn] manner, he was deeply kind.
words.nuance: Taciturn is a permanent trait of saying little, often seeming unfriendly. Laconic means using very few words, often with dry wit — it can be admiring.
words.ety: Latin taciturnus, from tacitus 'silent'.

prec.s: My ___ uncle could go a whole family holiday saying little more than 'yes' and 'no'.
prec.why: Taciturn describes a habit of hardly speaking at all. Reticent means reluctant to reveal something specific; introverted describes inward focus, not word count; diffident means lacking confidence.

words.def: Shy and lacking confidence in oneself.
ex: He was a [diffident] young man who hated speaking in public.
She offered her suggestion in a [diffident] tone, as if expecting rejection.
Behind his [diffidence] lay a brilliant mind.
words.nuance: Diffident specifically means lacking self-confidence, so hesitant to assert oneself. Timid adds fear; self-effacing means deliberately keeping a low profile; modest is about not boasting.
words.ety: Latin diffidere 'to mistrust', from dis- + fidere 'to trust' — not trusting oneself.

prec.s: Though highly talented, she was too ___ to put herself forward for promotion.
prec.why: Diffident means lacking confidence in oneself — exactly what stops her. Indifferent means not caring; reluctant means unwilling (for any reason); aloof means cool and distant.

words.def: Too eager to please or obey people in authority.
ex: The [obsequious] waiter kept bowing and calling him 'sir'.
Politicians were [obsequious] in their praise of the new leader.
I find his [obsequiousness] towards the boss embarrassing.
words.nuance: Obsequious focuses on excessive eagerness to serve and obey. Sycophantic focuses on flattery for personal gain. Servile suggests a slave-like lack of self-respect.
words.ety: Latin obsequi 'to comply with', from sequi 'to follow'.

prec.s: The hotel staff were almost ___, rushing to open doors and bowing at every request.
prec.why: Obsequious criticises an excessive, embarrassing eagerness to serve. Deferential (showing respect), courteous and attentive are all positive or neutral.

words.def: A person who flatters powerful people to gain advantage.
ex: The dictator surrounded himself with [sycophants] who never told him the truth.
Nobody likes a [sycophant], least of all the people he flatters.
The interview was embarrassingly [sycophantic].
words.nuance: A sycophant flatters to gain something. Yes-man is informal (someone who always agrees with the boss); toady is old-fashioned and contemptuous.
words.ety: Greek sukophantēs 'informer', of disputed origin.

prec.s: Instead of honest advisers, the king was surrounded by ___ who praised every decision.
prec.why: Sycophants flatter the powerful for advantage, which the sentence describes. Allies support you; acolytes are devoted followers; confidants are people you trust with secrets.

words.def: Behaving as if one is superior to others; scornfully arrogant.
ex: The [supercilious] shop assistant looked at my trainers and raised an eyebrow.
He gave a [supercilious] smile when I mispronounced the wine.
Critics found the film's tone [supercilious] towards ordinary people.
words.nuance: Supercilious is arrogance shown through facial expression and manner — the raised eyebrow. Condescending is treating someone as less intelligent; haughty is proud and cold.
words.ety: Latin supercilium 'eyebrow' — literally raising one's eyebrows at others.

prec.s: The sommelier raised one eyebrow with a ___ look when I asked for ice in my wine.
prec.why: Supercilious literally comes from 'eyebrow' and suits scornful looks. Condescending suits how someone talks down to you; pompous means self-important; imperious means domineering.

words.def: Very attentive to detail and accuracy; very concerned about cleanliness, sometimes excessively.
ex: He's [fastidious] about his appearance and irons even his T-shirts.
The restoration was carried out with [fastidious] attention to detail.
Cats are [fastidious] animals that spend hours cleaning themselves.
words.nuance: Fastidious can be praise (careful) or mild criticism (fussy, hard to please, especially about cleanliness and taste). Meticulous is always praise for careful work.
words.ety: Latin fastidiosus 'disdainful, squeamish', from fastidium 'loathing'.

prec.s: My ___ flatmate wipes down every surface twice and won't touch food others have handled.
prec.why: Fastidious includes the squeamish, hard-to-please concern with cleanliness. Meticulous, diligent and thorough describe careful work, not squeamishness.

words.def: Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise.
ex: The report is the result of [meticulous] research.
She kept [meticulous] records of every expense.
The crime was [meticulously] planned.
words.nuance: Meticulous is the all-purpose word for careful, precise work. Painstaking stresses the effort involved; scrupulous adds honesty and moral care.
words.ety: Latin meticulosus 'fearful', from metus 'fear' — originally 'timid', later 'careful'.

prec.s: Thanks to her ___ records, the accountant found the error in minutes.
prec.why: 'Meticulous records' are kept with precise attention to every detail. Pedantic criticises showing off minor knowledge; fastidious implies fussiness about cleanliness or taste; painstaking stresses the labour and collocates with effort or work, not records.

words.def: Showing great attention to details of correct behaviour, etiquette or procedure.
ex: He was [punctilious] about answering every letter within a day.
The ambassador was [punctilious] in observing diplomatic protocol.
She is [punctilious] about giving credit to her sources.
words.nuance: Punctilious is about rules of conduct, manners and duty — doing every 'point' correctly. Meticulous is about precise work; punctual (a related word) only means on time.
words.ety: Italian puntiglio 'small point', from Latin punctum 'point'.

prec.s: The old diplomat was ___ about etiquette, always addressing everyone by their proper title.
prec.why: Punctilious means careful about correct behaviour and protocol. Punctual means on time; pedantic means obsessed with minor rules of knowledge, showing off; prudish means easily shocked by sex.

words.def: Changing mood or behaviour suddenly and without reason; unpredictable.
ex: The [capricious] boss would praise you one day and fire you the next.
Farmers are at the mercy of [capricious] weather.
The decision seemed [capricious], with no clear reasoning behind it.
words.nuance: Capricious stresses impulsive changes driven by whim, not reason — decisions, rulers, weather. Fickle is used for changing loyalty or affection; mercurial for rapidly changing moods and temperament.
words.ety: French capricieux, from Italian capriccio 'sudden start', possibly from capra 'goat'.

prec.s: Employees lived in fear of the director's ___ decisions, which seemed to depend on her mood that morning.
prec.why: Capricious best describes decisions made on a whim, without reasoning. Fickle is about loyalty or affection; volatile about explosive moods or markets; erratic about irregular performance or movement.

words.def: Subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood; lively and quick.
ex: The [mercurial] striker could win a match alone or disappear for ninety minutes.
Working for such a [mercurial] director was exhausting.
Her [mercurial] temperament made her a brilliant but difficult actor.
words.nuance: Mercurial describes a person whose moods change quickly — often brilliant, charismatic and difficult at once. It can carry a hint of admiration that volatile lacks.
words.ety: From Mercury, the quick-witted Roman messenger god, and the liquid metal mercury.

prec.s: The band's ___ lead singer could be charming one minute and furious the next.
prec.why: Mercurial describes a lively personality with rapid mood swings. Fickle is about changing affections; arbitrary about decisions without reason; inconsistent about uneven quality.

words.def: Stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or behaviour; (of a problem) hard to deal with.
ex: He's too [obstinate] to admit he was wrong.
The children remained [obstinately] silent.
We finally removed the [obstinate] stain with vinegar.
words.nuance: Obstinate is close to stubborn but more critical and formal: refusing to change despite good reasons. Tenacious (positive) means persistent in pursuing a goal.
words.ety: Latin obstinare 'to persist', related to tenere 'to hold'.

prec.s: Despite all the evidence, he was too ___ to admit his mistake.
prec.why: Obstinate is the critical word for refusing to change despite good reason. Tenacious, resolute and steadfast are all positive — persistence and loyalty you'd admire.

words.def: Refusing to change one's views or to agree or compromise.
ex: Talks broke down because both sides remained [intransigent].
The union accused management of [intransigence].
His [intransigent] stance on immigration alienated moderate voters.
words.nuance: Intransigent is the classic word for negotiations and politics: refusing any compromise. Obstinate is more personal and everyday.
words.ety: Spanish los intransigentes, extreme republicans in the 1870s; from Latin transigere 'to come to an understanding'.

prec.s: The peace talks collapsed after both governments remained ___ on the question of borders.
prec.why: Intransigent is the standard word for parties in negotiations refusing to compromise. Obstinate is more personal; adamant means firmly insisting on a statement; determined is about pursuing a goal.

words.def: Willing to accept or be influenced by a suggestion; (of a thing) able to be treated in a particular way.
ex: The landlord seemed [amenable] to lowering the rent.
Most children are [amenable] to reason if you explain things calmly.
Some kinds of cancer are more [amenable] to treatment than others.
words.nuance: Amenable (to) means open to being persuaded — a positive, cooperative attitude. Compliant suggests obedience; receptive suggests willingness to consider ideas.
words.ety: Old French amener 'to bring to', from Latin minare 'to drive (animals)'.

prec.s: My boss is usually ___ to suggestions, as long as you bring data to support them.
prec.why: Amenable means open to being persuaded — cooperative but not weak. Submissive, obedient and docile all suggest yielding to authority without thought.

words.def: Friendly, good-natured and easy to talk to.
ex: The new manager is [affable] and approachable.
Behind his [affable] manner was a ruthless negotiator.
She chatted [affably] with the staff before the meeting.
words.nuance: Affable means pleasant and easy to approach, especially of someone in a higher position. Gregarious means loving company; amiable means friendly and likeable.
words.ety: Latin affabilis 'easy to speak to', from fari 'to speak'.

prec.s: Despite being the company's founder, he was ___ and happy to chat with interns in the lift.
prec.why: Affable describes someone easy to approach, notably someone senior. Gregarious means loving crowds; garrulous means talking too much; flamboyant means showy.

words.def: Truthful and straightforward, even when the truth is uncomfortable; (of photos) unposed.
ex: To be [candid], I don't think the plan will work.
She gave a [candid] interview about her struggle with depression.
The wedding album includes some lovely [candid] shots.
words.nuance: Candid suggests honesty that is welcome and sincere. Blunt adds a lack of tact; frank is close to candid but slightly more forceful; forthright means direct and outspoken.
words.ety: Latin candidus 'white, pure'.

prec.s: In a rare, ___ interview, the actor spoke openly about his addiction.
prec.why: Candid means honestly open about yourself — appreciated by the listener. Blunt and tactless imply hurting others; brusque means curt and abrupt.

words.def: Not sincere; pretending to know less or be more innocent than one really is.
ex: It's [disingenuous] of him to claim he didn't know about the deal.
Her surprise at the result was slightly [disingenuous].
The company's apology struck many customers as [disingenuous].
words.nuance: Disingenuous is subtler than lying: pretending ignorance or innocence, or making a misleading point while appearing fair. Duplicitous suggests active double-dealing.
words.ety: dis- + ingenuous 'innocent, frank', from Latin ingenuus 'native, freeborn'.

prec.s: It's ___ for the CEO to say he was shocked by the layoffs he personally approved.
prec.why: Disingenuous names exactly this: feigned innocence or surprise. Naive would mean he genuinely didn't know; deceitful and fraudulent imply active lying or criminal deception.

words.def: Deliberately deceitful; saying one thing and doing another.
ex: The [duplicitous] spy worked for both governments.
She felt betrayed by her [duplicitous] business partner.
The scandal exposed years of [duplicity] at the bank.
words.nuance: Duplicitous stresses doubleness — two faces, two loyalties. Treacherous adds betrayal of trust; two-faced is the informal equivalent.
words.ety: Latin duplex 'twofold'.

prec.s: The ___ agent had been passing secrets to both sides for a decade.
prec.why: Duplicitous fits a double game — working for two sides. Disingenuous is feigned innocence; hypocritical is preaching what you don't practise; devious is cunning in general.

words.def: Behaving as if one is morally superior to others.
ex: I'm tired of his [sanctimonious] lectures about recycling.
The article's [sanctimonious] tone put many readers off.
She hates [sanctimonious] people who judge others' parenting.
words.nuance: Sanctimonious is always negative: showy moral superiority. Self-righteous means convinced of one's own rightness; pious can be sincere religious devotion.
words.ety: Latin sanctimonia 'sanctity', from sanctus 'holy'.

prec.s: He drives a huge car, yet gives everyone ___ lectures about their carbon footprint.
prec.why: Sanctimonious mocks moralising from someone acting superior. Pious and devout can be sincere religious devotion; earnest means serious and sincere.

words.def: Not wanting to draw attention to oneself or one's achievements; modest.
ex: The [self-effacing] scientist gave all the credit to her team.
His [self-effacing] humour made him popular with audiences.
Despite her fame, she remained shy and [self-effacing].
words.nuance: Self-effacing means actively keeping oneself in the background, often charmingly. Modest means not boasting; diffident implies lack of confidence; unassuming means not pretentious.
words.ety: efface 'rub out', from French effacer, from face — to erase oneself.

prec.s: Despite leading the project, she was ___, crediting her team in every interview and avoiding the cameras.
prec.why: Self-effacing means keeping oneself modestly in the background. Self-conscious means awkwardly aware of being watched; self-absorbed means preoccupied with oneself; self-assured means confident.

words.def: Too satisfied with oneself or a situation, and therefore not careful enough about possible dangers.
ex: After three easy wins, the team became [complacent] and lost.
We can't afford to be [complacent] about cybersecurity.
Success had bred [complacency] in the company.
words.nuance: Complacent stresses the danger of relaxing too much. Smug stresses an annoying, self-satisfied attitude. Don't confuse with complaisant (eager to please).
words.ety: Latin complacere 'to please greatly', from placere 'to please'.

prec.s: Two years without a security breach made the IT team ___, and they stopped installing updates.
prec.why: Complacent is the word for relaxing your guard because things are going well. Smug is about annoying self-satisfaction; content is simply happy; conceited means vain.

words.def: Wanting to avoid activity or effort; lazy.
ex: They spent an [indolent] summer lying by the pool.
Critics described the [indolent] aristocrats who never worked a day.
His teachers blamed his poor grades on [indolence], not lack of ability.
words.nuance: Indolent is a literary word for habitual laziness, sometimes describing a pleasant, relaxed mood. Lethargic means lacking energy (often from illness or tiredness), not unwillingness.
words.ety: Late Latin indolens 'not feeling pain', from dolere 'to suffer'.

prec.s: The novel portrays the ___ rich, who spend their days lounging on yachts doing nothing at all.
prec.why: Indolent means habitually lazy by preference. Lethargic, sluggish and listless suggest low energy or illness, not a lifestyle choice.

words.def: Showing great care, attention and persistent effort.
ex: Thanks to her [assiduous] research, the case was reopened.
He [assiduously] avoided any mention of the scandal.
The garden was the result of years of [assiduous] care.
words.nuance: Assiduous emphasises constant, persevering attention. Diligent is the more common word for careful hard work. 'Assiduously avoid' is a useful ironic collocation.
words.ety: Latin assiduus 'constantly present', from assidere 'to sit beside', from sedere.

prec.s: For a year, the minister ___ avoided giving any interviews about the scandal.
prec.why: 'Assiduously avoid' is a fixed collocation for persistent, deliberate avoidance. Diligently and industriously suggest productive work; zealously suggests passionate enthusiasm.

words.def: Holding firmly to something; very determined and persistent.
ex: A [tenacious] journalist spent five years uncovering the scandal.
The team showed great [tenacity] in coming back from 2–0 down.
Old habits are [tenacious].
words.nuance: Tenacious is admiring: refusing to give up or let go. Dogged stresses stubborn, unglamorous persistence; obstinate is negative.
words.ety: Latin tenax 'holding fast', from tenere 'to hold'.

prec.s: A ___ reporter, she followed the story for six years until the truth came out.
prec.why: Tenacious is admiring persistence towards a goal. Obstinate, stubborn and headstrong criticise refusing to change your mind.

words.def: Showing a willingness to take surprisingly bold risks; (negatively) shamelessly bold.
ex: It was an [audacious] plan to rob the bank in broad daylight.
The architect's [audacious] design divided critics.
He had the [audacity] to ask for a pay rise after missing the deadline.
words.nuance: Audacious can be admiring (daring, original) or critical (cheeky). 'Have the audacity to' is always critical. Intrepid means fearless in facing danger, especially explorers.
words.ety: Latin audax 'bold', from audere 'to dare'.

prec.s: The startup announced an ___ plan to put a hotel on the Moon within a decade.
prec.why: Audacious suits a surprisingly bold plan or goal. Intrepid and valiant describe people facing danger; foolhardy means recklessly stupid, a harsher judgement.

words.def: Bold and without shame; (v. brazen it out) to face trouble shamelessly.
ex: It was a [brazen] lie, told in front of witnesses.
Thieves [brazenly] stole the statue during a public event.
Caught red-handed, he decided to [brazen] it out.
words.nuance: Brazen is always negative: bold without shame or embarrassment. Flagrant describes the offence (obvious and serious), brazen the attitude of the offender.
words.ety: Old English bræsen 'made of brass' — hard and shameless.

prec.s: In a ___ act of theft, the gang drove a truck through the shop window at midday.
prec.why: Brazen means shamelessly bold, unconcerned about being seen. Audacious can be admiring; covert and furtive mean secret — the opposite.

words.def: Acting quickly and without thinking about the consequences.
ex: In an [impetuous] moment, he quit his job and booked a flight to Bali.
Her [impetuous] decision to marry after two weeks shocked everyone.
Young and [impetuous], he often regretted what he said in anger.
words.nuance: Impetuous suggests energy and emotion carrying someone away — often young people. Rash stresses lack of judgement; impulsive means acting on sudden urges.
words.ety: Latin impetus 'attack, force', from petere 'to seek, attack'.

prec.s: Young and ___, Romeo marries Juliet within a day of meeting her.
prec.why: Impetuous means acting on passion without thought. Impervious means unaffected; impertinent means rude; imperious means arrogantly commanding.

words.def: Acting with care and thought for the future.
ex: It would be [prudent] to get a second opinion before surgery.
[Prudent] investors spread their money across different assets.
Financial [prudence] means saving for a rainy day.
words.nuance: Prudent focuses on caution and avoiding future risk, especially with money. Judicious focuses on good judgement in a specific choice. Careful: 'prudish' is a different word (easily shocked by sex).
words.ety: Latin prudens, contraction of providens 'foreseeing'.

prec.s: With a recession expected, it would be ___ to build up some savings now.
prec.why: Prudent means wisely cautious about the future. Prudish means easily shocked by sexual matters; impudent means cheeky and disrespectful; judicial relates to courts and judges.

words.def: Having or showing good judgement, especially in choosing or using something.
ex: A [judicious] use of colour can transform a small room.
With some [judicious] editing, the report could be half the length.
She used her influence [judiciously].
words.nuance: Judicious is ideal for wise, measured use of something ('judicious use of humour'). Don't confuse with judicial (relating to courts and judges).
words.ety: French judicieux, from Latin iudicium 'judgement'.

prec.s: A ___ use of humour can make even a technical presentation enjoyable.
prec.why: 'Judicious use of' is the natural collocation: wise, well-measured use. Judicial relates to courts; prudent is about caution and risk; shrewd is about clever, self-interested judgement.

words.def: Having or showing sharp practical judgement, especially to gain an advantage.
ex: She's a [shrewd] businesswoman who never overpays.
It was a [shrewd] move to buy property before the area became popular.
I have a [shrewd] idea who sent the anonymous letter.
words.nuance: Shrewd mixes intelligence with practical, sometimes self-interested cunning. Astute is more neutral and intellectual; canny is informal; savvy is informal and modern.
words.ety: Middle English shrewe 'evil person' — originally 'malicious', later 'cunning', then 'clever'.

prec.s: A ___ negotiator, he always got the other side to name a price first.
prec.why: Shrewd describes practical, tactical cleverness used for advantage. Wise is about deep good judgement; learned and erudite are about book knowledge.

words.def: Able to assess situations or people accurately and turn this to one's advantage.
ex: That's a very [astute] observation.
An [astute] politician, she knew exactly when to stay silent.
He [astutely] predicted the collapse of the housing market.
words.nuance: Astute is praise for sharp perception and judgement. 'An astute observation' is a typical compliment in discussions. Shrewd is more about cunning in practical dealings.
words.ety: Latin astutus 'cunning', from astus 'craft'.

prec.s: 'That's a very ___ observation,' said the professor, impressed by the student's point.
prec.why: Astute is the natural compliment for an insightful remark. Cunning, crafty and wily suggest tricks and deceit.

words.def: Too ready to believe things; easily deceived.
ex: Scammers target [credulous] people with promises of easy money.
The documentary was criticised for its [credulous] treatment of conspiracy theories.
The story strains [credulity].
words.nuance: Credulous is the formal word for gullible. Incredulous is the opposite feeling (unable to believe). Credible means believable — a frequent confusion.
words.ety: Latin credulus 'trusting', from credere 'to believe'.

prec.s: Only the most ___ readers believed the article about aliens building the pyramids.
prec.why: Credulous means believing too easily. Credible means believable; incredulous means unable to believe; creditable means deserving praise.

words.def: Bored, tired or cynical after having too much of something.
ex: After twenty years in politics, she had become [jaded] and cynical.
This dish will impress even the most [jaded] palate.
[Jaded] by endless meetings, he stopped paying attention.
words.nuance: Jaded implies that too much experience has dulled enthusiasm. Blasé implies unimpressed indifference (sometimes a pose); cynical implies distrust of people's motives.
words.ety: From jade 'a worn-out horse'.

prec.s: Having reviewed restaurants for thirty years, the critic had a ___ palate that few chefs could impress.
prec.why: Jaded means dulled by too much experience — 'a jaded palate' is a set phrase. Sceptical means doubtful; apathetic means not caring at all; disillusioned means disappointed after losing an ideal.

words.def: Childishly sulky or bad-tempered.
ex: The player kicked the ball away in a [petulant] display after the red card.
Stop being so [petulant] — you can't always get what you want.
She closed the laptop with a [petulant] sigh.
words.nuance: Petulant suggests a childish, sulky reaction to not getting one's way. Irascible means easily angered (a trait); peevish means irritable over small things.
words.ety: Latin petulans 'impudent', from petere 'to seek, attack'.

prec.s: When his idea was rejected, the CEO stormed out like a ___ toddler.
prec.why: Petulant is the word for childish sulking. Irascible describes someone with a quick temper generally; belligerent means aggressive and hostile; querulous means complaining in a whining way.

words.def: Having a tendency to be easily angered.
ex: The [irascible] old professor shouted at anyone who arrived late.
He was famously [irascible] but deeply loyal.
Lack of sleep made her [irascible].
words.nuance: Irascible is a permanent tendency to anger quickly — often used affectionately for grumpy elderly characters. Cantankerous adds argumentativeness.
words.ety: Latin irasci 'to grow angry', from ira 'anger'.

prec.s: The ___ chef was known for throwing pans whenever anything went wrong in the kitchen.
prec.why: Irascible describes a personality quick to explode in anger. Petulant is childish sulking; pugnacious is eager to fight or argue; sullen is silent and resentful.

words.def: Enduring pain or hardship calmly, without showing feelings or complaining.
ex: She remained [stoic] throughout her long illness.
He accepted the news with [stoic] calm.
Fans have shown remarkable [stoicism] through years of defeats.
words.nuance: Stoic implies strength in enduring suffering without complaint. Resigned implies giving up; phlegmatic is a calm temperament generally, not necessarily under suffering.
words.ety: From the Stoics, Greek philosophers who taught at the Stoa (porch) in Athens.

prec.s: Through months of painful treatment, he remained ___, never once complaining.
prec.why: Stoic is about enduring pain without complaint. Apathetic and indifferent mean not caring; phlegmatic is a calm temperament in general, not specifically endurance of suffering.

words.def: Showing selfless concern for the well-being of others.
ex: Was his donation purely [altruistic], or did he want publicity?
Some animals show surprisingly [altruistic] behaviour.
She became a nurse out of [altruism], not for the money.
words.nuance: Altruistic emphasises motive: helping others with no benefit to yourself. Philanthropic refers to giving money to good causes, often on a large scale.
words.ety: French altruisme, from Italian altrui 'somebody else'.

prec.s: Critics doubted that the billionaire's motives were truly ___; the donation came with a tax break and his name on a building.
prec.why: Altruistic is specifically about selfless motives — the point under question. Philanthropic and charitable describe the act of giving; generous describes the size of the gift.

words.def: Willing to act dishonestly in return for money; corrupt.
ex: [Venal] officials were paid to ignore safety violations.
The novel satirises a [venal] press that prints anything for money.
The regime was notorious for its [venality].
words.nuance: Venal specifically means open to bribery. Don't confuse with venial (a venial sin is a minor, forgivable one). Mercenary means motivated only by money.
words.ety: Latin venalis 'for sale', from venum 'sale'.

prec.s: The inspector was so ___ that a few hundred dollars was enough to get any building approved.
prec.why: Venal means open to bribery. Venial means minor and forgivable; venerable means respected because of age; vengeful means seeking revenge.

words.def: Self-important and solemn; trying to seem grand.
ex: The [pompous] speaker went on for an hour about his own achievements.
Her writing is clear, never [pompous].
He was mocked for his [pomposity].
words.nuance: Pompous mocks someone who takes himself too seriously. Pretentious is pretending to be more important or cultured than you are; bombastic is about inflated language.
words.ety: Latin pompa 'procession, pomp'.

prec.s: The ___ mayor insisted on being called 'Your Worship' and gave hour-long speeches about himself.
prec.why: Pompous captures solemn self-importance — titles, long speeches. Haughty is cold pride; bombastic describes inflated language specifically; arrogant is broader overconfidence.

words.def: Having or showing great knowledge gained from study.
ex: She gave an [erudite] lecture on medieval music.
The book is [erudite] but surprisingly easy to read.
His [erudition] was matched only by his kindness.
words.nuance: Erudite is praise for deep, wide learning, especially in the humanities. Pedantic is the negative side: showing off knowledge or obsessing over minor details.
words.ety: Latin eruditus 'instructed', from erudire 'to train', literally 'to bring out of roughness'.

prec.s: An ___ scholar, she could quote Latin poets and Arabic philosophers with equal ease.
prec.why: Erudite means deeply learned through study. Pedantic is a criticism; intelligent is about ability, not knowledge; literate merely means able to read and write.

words.def: Too concerned with minor details or rules, especially in showing off knowledge.
ex: I don't want to be [pedantic], but 'less' should be 'fewer' here.
His [pedantic] corrections annoyed everyone at the meeting.
The review is full of [pedantry] about footnotes.
col: at the risk of being pedantic
words.nuance: Pedantic criticises showing off knowledge through trivial corrections. Punctilious is about correct behaviour and duty, often neutral or positive.
words.ety: Italian pedante 'teacher', possibly from Greek paideuein 'to teach'.

prec.s: At the risk of sounding ___, the war ended in 1945, not 1946.
prec.why: 'At the risk of sounding pedantic' is the stock phrase before correcting a minor factual detail. The others describe careful conduct or work, not annoying corrections.

words.def: Peculiar to an individual; distinctive and unusual.
ex: He has an [idiosyncratic] way of spelling, but his ideas are brilliant.
The museum reflects the founder's [idiosyncratic] taste.
Every writer has their [idiosyncrasies].
words.nuance: Idiosyncratic describes something personal and unusual, without the judgement of eccentric (odd behaviour) or quirky (charmingly odd, informal).
words.ety: Greek idiosunkrasia, from idios 'own' + sunkrasis 'mixture'.

prec.s: The film critic's rankings are ___: she loves obscure 1970s horror and hates most Oscar winners.
prec.why: Idiosyncratic means reflecting one person's distinctive, unusual tastes. Erratic means irregular and unpredictable; arbitrary means without reason; eclectic means drawn from many sources.

words.def: Not friendly or forthcoming; cool and distant.
ex: Some colleagues find her [aloof], but she's just shy.
The president remained [aloof] from the debate.
His [aloofness] made it hard to get to know him.
words.nuance: Aloof is about keeping emotional distance, which others may read as coldness or superiority. Reserved is milder (slow to reveal feelings); standoffish is informal and critical.
words.ety: From a- 'on' + luff (sailing) — keeping a ship's head to the wind, away from the shore.

prec.s: The new director stayed ___ from the staff, eating lunch alone in her office and rarely chatting.
prec.why: 'Remain aloof from' people describes a cool, unapproachable manner. Detached suggests emotional uninvolvement or objectivity; secluded and isolated describe physical separation.

words.def: Trying too hard to make people like you, especially by flattery.
ex: He gave the manager an [ingratiating] smile.
She tried to [ingratiate] herself with the new boss by bringing him coffee every morning.
His tone was polite, almost [ingratiating].
words.nuance: Ingratiating is about trying to win favour — the manner, the smile. Obsequious stresses servility; sycophantic stresses flattery of the powerful; unctuous adds oily, insincere charm.
words.ety: Latin in gratiam 'into favour', from gratia 'grace'.

prec.s: On his first day he gave the boss an ___ smile and laughed a little too loudly at her jokes.
prec.why: Ingratiating describes behaviour designed to win favour, and it is critical — 'a little too loudly' signals that. Endearing, engaging and winning are positive: genuinely charming.
